title: The £80B PFI bill NHS hospitals are still paying
narrative_md:
**Forty English hospitals built for £12 billion will cost the NHS over £80 billion before the last contract expires in 2050.**

The Private Finance Initiative built around 102 NHS hospitals between 1997 and 2017, for a combined construction value of roughly £12 billion. The lifetime cost of servicing those contracts — annual 'unitary charge' payments running to 2050 and beyond — is over £80 billion. In 2024-25 alone, NHS trusts will pay £2.1 billion in PFI charges.

PFI was sold as off-balance-sheet capital: private consortia would design, build, operate and maintain hospitals, charging the NHS an annual fee over 25-30 years. The political attraction in the late 1990s was clear — new hospitals without new Treasury borrowing. The fiscal reality, two decades on, is that PFI financed at 7-9% what government could have borrowed at 4-5%. The spread compounds.

The Centre for Health and the Public Interest estimates that PFI unitary charges for NHS trusts peaked at £2.2 billion in 2022-23 and remain near that level. For individual trusts the effects can be devastating: Calderdale and Huddersfield NHS Foundation Trust pays roughly 15% of its operating expenditure to PFI; UCLH was similar in the mid-2010s before active renegotiation. Barts Health NHS Trust's Royal London Hospital PFI alone costs £115 million a year.

The contracts were badly designed on the NHS side. Many include RPI-linked indexation (RPI has consistently exceeded CPI since 2010), performance deductions that rarely bite, and hard facilities-management contracts that prevent trusts from switching catering or cleaning suppliers for decades. 'Soft FM' contracts — for example, the cost of changing a lightbulb at a PFI hospital in Norfolk — became parliamentary set-pieces in the 2010s.

The Treasury stopped signing new PFI contracts in 2018 after a decade of NAO criticism. But the tail is long. Most NHS PFI deals run 30 years from construction, meaning contracts signed in 2005 expire in 2035; contracts signed in 2015 expire in 2045. The latest current deal — Royal Liverpool — expires in 2050.

Renegotiation has been limited. A small number of trusts have bought out PFI contracts early where the breakage cost was favourable, but most cannot afford the lump-sum exit. The 2024-25 Autumn Budget flagged a 'PFI exit review' in DHSC, but no fiscal envelope was announced. Treasury officials privately argue that PFI buyouts would trigger a £15-25 billion fiscal event for a saving only realised over 15 years.

The hidden story is maintenance. PFI contracts typically transferred lifecycle maintenance risk to the private consortium. As those contracts approach expiry, the condition of the buildings returning to NHS ownership is variable. A National Audit Office survey in 2024 identified 14 PFI hospitals with 'significant unresolved maintenance backlogs' expected to return to NHS accounts on contract expiry — potentially adding £3-5 billion to the £13 billion NHS maintenance backlog already on the books.

For new hospital building, Labour's New Hospital Programme (reviewed in January 2025) will rely on direct capital funding rather than PFI. But that funding is constrained by the same debt interest bill that made PFI attractive in the 1990s. The irony is that PFI was invented to avoid the very fiscal rules that now make PFI look expensive.
